```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(readr)
library(dplyr)

rtheme <- reactableTheme(
  borderColor    = "rgba(30,40,51,0.18)",
  highlightColor = "#ECE6D9",

                        fontSize = "13px"))
```

Every dataset here is public and free, with no login and no paid access. Where a source would normally mean accepting terms or doing a manual download, I kept a small table in the repo instead. If you want to extend the project, the notes below say what to swap in.

## Base geography

Country shapes and coastlines come from **Natural Earth**, loaded through the `rnaturalearth` package. Natural Earth is in the public domain, and the package ships with the data, which means there is nothing to download by hand.

## Energy infrastructure

The infrastructure layer is a small table of the region's LNG (liquefied natural gas) import terminals, `data/processed/lng_terminals.csv`. For each terminal it holds the name, country, location, annual import capacity (in billion cubic metres, or bcm), status and a source note. You can sort or search it here:

```{r terminals-table}
#| echo: false
read_csv("data/processed/lng_terminals.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  transmute(Terminal = name, Country = country,
            `Capacity (bcm)` = capacity_bcm, Status = status,
            Type = type, Source = source) |>
  reactable(sortable = TRUE, searchable = TRUE, highlight = TRUE,
            borderless = TRUE, pagination = FALSE, theme = rtheme,
            columns = list(Source = colDef(minWidth = 220)))
```

[Download this table as a CSV](data/processed/lng_terminals.csv)

I took the capacities from operator reporting and the **Global Energy Monitor** terminal tracker, current as of 2024 to 2025, and the `source` column in the table names the operator behind each figure. I would flag two points:

- Capacities move, and a headline figure is often the planned one. Świnoujście only reached 8.3 bcm in January 2025, once its third tank came online. Mukran is often quoted at 13.5 bcm, but that figure assumes two FSRUs (the moored ships that store and re-gasify LNG). Deutsche ReGas ended the charter on the second unit, and the terminal now runs on one ship, the Neptune, which is why I count it here at about 6 bcm. Taking the 13.5 figure at face value would roughly double Germany's seaborne supply on paper.
- I left the Paldiski jetty in Estonia out on purpose. It is shelved, and its capacity figure refers to the same ship (the Exemplar) that now operates at Inkoo. Including both would count one vessel twice.

Anyone extending the project could add the pipelines and cables as mapped routes from **EMODnet Human Activities** and **OpenStreetMap** (via the `osmdata` package), and check the full set of capacities against the **Global Energy Monitor** tracker.

## Transit corridors

The corridor map on the Analysis page uses a small table, `data/processed/transit_lines.csv`, which lists the main subsea pipelines and cables by their landing points and status. I drew them as **schematic straight lines**. They are not surveyed routes. What I wanted to show is which corridors exist and which have been disrupted, and the exact path matters less for that. Positions and dates come from operator and press reporting. The true routes could be mapped by adding the actual route lines from **EMODnet Human Activities** or **OpenStreetMap**.

## Proximity reference

For proximity I used distance to the nearest **Russian territory** instead of a maritime boundary line. That covers the mainland near the Gulf of Finland plus the Kaliningrad exclave, taken from Natural Earth. Anyone can reproduce it from a public package, and it is easy to read, since it is simply how far each terminal is from Russian soil.

## Dependence

The dependence layer uses gas import dependency from **Eurostat** (indicator `nrg_ind_id`, natural gas, 2023), held in `data/processed/import_dependence.csv`. The figure is the share of gas demand met by net imports. Where a value goes above 100%, it reflects stock draws or re-exports in that year. Denmark is low because it has its own North Sea production. `scripts/03_eurostat.R` reproduces the pull.

```{r dependence-table}
#| echo: false
read_csv("data/processed/import_dependence.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  transmute(Country = country,
            `Import dependency (%)` = gas_import_dependency_pct) |>
  arrange(desc(`Import dependency (%)`)) |>
  reactable(sortable = TRUE, highlight = TRUE, borderless = TRUE,
            pagination = FALSE, theme = rtheme)
```

[Download this table as a CSV](data/processed/import_dependence.csv)

The table above is committed 2023 data. For comparison, the figure below is pulled
live from the Eurostat API in your browser when this page loads:

::: {#live-dependency style="font-size:0.95em;color:#5E6875;margin-top:0.5rem"}
Checking Eurostat for the latest EU-wide figure...
:::

```{=html}
<script>
(function () {
  var el = document.getElementById('live-dependency');
  if (!el) return;
  var url = 'https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/api/dissemination/statistics/1.0/data/nrg_ind_id'
          + '?format=JSON&lang=EN&freq=A&siec=G3000&unit=PC&geo=EU27_2020&lastTimePeriod=1';
  fetch(url).then(function (r) { return r.json(); }).then(function (d) {
    var year = Object.values(d.dimension.time.category.label)[0];
    var val  = Object.values(d.value)[0];
    el.textContent = "Live from Eurostat: the EU's gas import dependency for natural "
                   + "gas in " + year + " was " + val.toFixed(1) + "%.";
  }).catch(function () {
    el.textContent = "The live Eurostat figure is unavailable right now; the table "
                   + "above shows the committed 2023 data.";
  });
})();
</script>
```

## Gas demand

To judge whether the terminals are big enough, I compare their capacity with what each country actually burns. The demand figure is inland gas consumption from **Eurostat** (indicator `nrg_cb_gas`, natural gas, 2023), held in `data/processed/gas_demand.csv`. I converted it from million cubic metres to bcm to put it on the same scale as terminal capacity. `scripts/03_eurostat.R` pulls it alongside the dependency figures.

One caveat is that 2023 demand was itself depressed by high prices and mild weather across much of Europe. Against a colder year with higher demand, the coverage would look less comfortable.

[Download the demand figures as a CSV](data/processed/gas_demand.csv)

## Russian pipeline imports

For the before and after comparison I used imports of natural gas from Russia by pipeline, from **Eurostat** (indicator `nrg_ti_gas`, partner Russia, natural gas), for 2021 and 2023. They are held in `data/processed/russian_imports.csv` and converted to bcm. I use 2021 as the last full year before the invasion.

These are recorded imports rather than pipeline capacity, and I think that makes for the fairer comparison. Capacity figures for pipelines like Nord Stream describe what could have flowed. What these particular countries actually took is a different number.

[Download the import figures as a CSV](data/processed/russian_imports.csv)

## Why there is no conflict event layer

I framed this around exposure and structural dependence instead of active conflict. There is no battlefield on the Baltic seabed. I left ACLED out on purpose. It now requires registration, which would break the public data rule. If a later version needs conflict events, UCDP GED is the public, no-login substitute.

## How the data is prepared

The steps that turn the raw tables and map data into the layers behind the maps are in `scripts/01_clean.R`. The Analysis page runs the same steps each time it builds:

- tidy up the columns,
- put everything on a map projection suited to Europe, so distances come out in
  kilometres rather than degrees,
- trim the map to the Baltic study area,
- keep the capacity and country information attached to each terminal.

- Eurostat. Supply, transformation and consumption of gas, indicator
  `nrg_cb_gas`, inland consumption, natural gas, 2023.
  <https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat> (accessed August 2026).
- Eurostat. Imports of natural gas by partner country, indicator `nrg_ti_gas`,
  partner Russia, 2021 and 2023. <https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat>
  (accessed August 2026).
- Global Energy Monitor. Global LNG Terminal Tracker.
  <https://globalenergymonitor.org> (accessed June 2026).
- Operator figures for capacity and status: Gaz-System, Deutsche ReGas, Gasgrid
  Finland, KN Energies, and Hamina LNG (2024 to 2025 reporting).

For adding pipelines or cables later, the sources are EMODnet Human Activities (<https://emodnet.ec.europa.eu/en/human-activities>) and OpenStreetMap.
